Balances
BAL-an-sez
noun (plural)
From the Latin bilanx — bis, twice, and lanx, a plate or scale — the two-pan scale. The word is plural in form because the instrument is double: two pans, one truth, and no verdict possible without both.

Biblical Definition

The balances are Scripture’s standing image of judgment, and the law treats their honesty as a matter of the LORD’s own name: “Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Lev 19:36). The reason attached is redemption — a people bought out of Egypt do not cheat in the marketplace. Solomon states the matter as strongly as anything in Proverbs: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Pro 11:1). Note the two words: not merely displeasing but abomination, and not merely acceptable but delight. God takes personal pleasure in an honest shopkeeper. Job, protesting his integrity, asks for the instrument to be used on him: “Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity” (Job 31:6) — a bold request, and one the book does not condemn. And the image reaches its terrible fulfilment on a wall in Babylon, where a hand wrote three words and Daniel read the second: “TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Dan 5:27). Belshazzar had drunk from the vessels of the temple that night. He was weighed the same night, and slain in it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A pair of scales for weighing; in Scripture the emblem of just dealing in trade and of God’s judgment of men.

BALANCE, n. A pair of scales; an instrument for ascertaining the weight of bodies.

From the Latin bilanx, from bis, twice, and lanx, a plate or dish.

The instrument consists of a beam suspended at its middle with a scale at each end.

Figuratively, the means of estimating or comparing; as, to weigh in the balance.

In Scripture, the emblem of just weight in commerce (Lev 19:36) and of divine judgment (Dan 5:27).

Key Scripture

Lev 19:36 — "Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt."

Pro 11:1 — "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight."

Job 31:6 — "Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity."

Dan 5:27 — "TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting."

Modern Corruption

Commercial honesty is filed under business ethics rather than worship, though Scripture attaches the just weight directly to God’s name, His delight, and the exodus itself.

expand to see more

The corruption is the partition of life into sacred and commercial. Weights and measures feel like a technical matter, properly governed by regulation and competition rather than by piety, and a man may be devout on Sunday and sharp on Monday without ever noticing a contradiction. Scripture makes no such division. Lev 19:36 puts just balances in the same chapter as loving thy neighbour as thyself and reverencing the sanctuary, and it grounds them all in one sentence: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt. Redemption is the reason for an honest scale. Pro 11:1 then raises the temperature: a false balance is abomination, a word Scripture reserves for idolatry and the grossest sins, while a just weight is God’s delight.

Recover the plain sense: the balance is where doctrine becomes visible to people who will never hear you preach. Every trade has its equivalent of the thumb on the scale — the padded invoice, the quiet substitution, the disclosed-in-small-print charge, the hour billed and not worked — and each is a small liturgy declaring what its author believes about God. Then let Dan 5:27 do its work. Belshazzar was weighed, and the instrument he was weighed in was the very one the law had commanded him to keep honest. Men who spend a life adjusting the scale should consider that they will one day stand in it, and that the hand which writes on the wall does not require a second opinion.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin bilanx, two-panned — the scale; emblem of just trade and of the judgment in which Belshazzar was found wanting.
